pages.x: A Temco controller speaks BACnet so that a building supervisor can read it without knowing anything about Temco tools. This version documents the object model and the addresses; the wiring is Test1's business. What a supervisor sees Every point the controller holds is an object with an instance number. A supervisor reads a point by asking for its object identifier, which is the type and the number

A point is an object with a type and an instance. This version exposes the types below; anything not listed is not reachable over BACnet, however visible it is in the tool. The types Type Name What it holds 0 Analog input A measured value: a temperature, a pressure, a 0–10 V signal 1 Analog output A value the supervisor may write, such as a setpoint 3 Binary input A switch or a proven state 4 Bina

Test1 is the controller every later Temco product was measured against: a small, fixed set of inputs and outputs, one program, and a display that says what the machine is doing. This documentation covers the version you are holding, and nothing else — each version keeps its own pages, so a machine commissioned two years ago still reads correctly. Work through this page at the machine, not at a desk. It takes about ten minutes and ends with a controller that answers, which is the state every other page assumes. Note Work at the controller, not at a desk: the driver install needs the machine plugged in, and the last step asks the hardware a question rather than the software. Install the driver The driver ships inside the Temco installer. Run

The controller has the same terminals on every model in the family. The numbers are printed beside them; the words below are what they do. The terminals Terminal Name What it is for 1–8 Universal inputs A switch, a sensor or a 0–10 V signal; the tool decides which 9–14 Digital outputs Relays, 24 V AC or DC, one amp each 15–16 Analog outputs 0–10 V, for a damper or a valve 17–18 Power 24 V AC, eith

A program is a list of lines the controller runs top to bottom, ten times a second. That is the whole model: no tasks, no threads, and no reason to fear it. The shape of a program Text Copy 10 IF IN1 = ON THEN OUT1 = ON 20 IF IN1 = OFF THEN OUT1 = OFF 30 IF AI1 > 22.5 THEN OUT2 = ON Every program worth keeping has three parts: what it reads, what it decides, and what it writes. pages.t: Alarms and how to clear them
h: The three that come up most
pages.x: An alarm is a sentence the controller writes when a value crosses a limit it was given. It is not a diagnosis, and it is not a fault: it is a fact with a time beside it. The log The controller keeps the last 100 alarms in order. Each entry holds the time, the alarm, and whether it has since cleared.
